title: 10 Disturbing Crimes in South Carolina History
fullText: Number one, Donald Henry Gaskins. To the neighbors who saw him in the fields of Florence County, he was a small, polite, hard-working man in a battered hat, a man whose feet did not quite reach the pedals of the trucks he drove, and whose voice never rose above a soft Carolina. Draw. He was called pee-wee for a reason. He stood barely 5'5 in tall. He shook hands with grandmothers at the general store. He fixed cars for pennies on the dollar. He was the sort of man other men trusted with their daughters rides home because he seemed too little, too quiet, too unremarkable to be anything but harmless. That is the first and most disturbing fact about Donald Henry Gaskins. To almost everyone who ever met him casually, he was not merely ordinary. He was beneath notice. And it was beneath notice that he committed the worst string of murders in South Carolina's recorded criminal history. Gaskins was born on March 13th, 1933 in the Pine Flats near Prospect, a scatter of dirt roads in Florence County that even most South Carolinians could not find on a map. His mother had a series of relationships with violent men. He was the fifth of her children, none by the same father, and none of them wanted the small, thin boy who was always in the way. He was called by junior parrot as a child, then simply pee-wee because the schoolyard bullies could not resist a target that small. He was hit at home. He was hit at school. He was hit on the roads by drunk men returning from the mill. By his own account, the world taught him early that everyone smaller than everyone else existed to be beaten, and the only escape from that arithmetic was to find someone smaller still. He dropped out of school by fourth grade. By 11, he was breaking into houses with two older boys. By 13, he was in juvenile detention for attacking a girl with a hatchet during a burglary gone wrong. And by the time he was sent to the South Carolina Industrial School for Boys, other inmates were already learning the strange thing about Pee-Wee Gaskins, the thing that would define him for the next four decades. He looked like nothing. But when he was cornered or humiliated or simply bored, something behind his eyes would slide sideways, and the small, polite boy would be gone, and something else would be looking out. For years after his release, that something else stayed hidden. Gaskins married young. He worked odd jobs. He fathered children. He attended, when it suited him, a small country church, sat quietly in the pews, and nodded at the sermons. He was known around Prospect as a man who could patch a roof cheaper than anyone else, and who could be counted on to give a stranded traveler a ride if the traveler did not mind the smell of oil in the cab of his Chevy. He appeared to be exactly what rural Florence County wanted him to be, a poor, harmless, useful little man. Underneath, the arithmetic was already turning. Gaskins would later tell a biographer that beginning in 1969, he began experiencing what he called bothersomeness, a pressure that built behind his eyes until it could only be relieved by killing. He did not describe it as rage. He described it as household maintenance, something that had to be attended to the way other men attended to broken fences. The mask he wore in public was almost surgical in its precision. When Gaskins picked up hitchhikers along Highway 17 or the narrow two lanes cutting through the Low Country, he was chatty, apologetic, self- aacing. He told women he had a wife and kids at home. He told men he was on his way to a job. He offered cigarettes. He offered gas money. He complimented rings, watches, boots. He drove them in his mind toward what he privately called his coastal kills. These were victims chosen almost at random from the ribbon of Southern Highway that unspooled between Charleston and the North Carolina line. To Gaskins they were, in his own chilling words, just people I didn't know. He shot them, stabbed them, or drowned them in the marsh, and he waited them into black water where the tide and the crabs would erase what he had done. But the mask had a second layer, one that made Gaskins uniquely dangerous, even among serial killers. Alongside the coastal kills, he committed what he called his serious murders. a private and premeditated category reserved for people he knew. People who had crossed him, people who had witnessed something, people whose insurance policies could be redirected, girlfriends of associates, nieces of enemies, small town rivals whose disappearances would be quietly explained away by the assumption that they had run off to Myrtle Beach or gotten mixed up with the wrong crowd. Gaskins buried these victims on land he was farming near Prospect. He would stand at a grave, brush the loose dirt with the toe of his boot, and go home to eat supper with his family. Neighbors who lived across the tobacco fields from him would later say the same thing over and over to reporters who came asking. He waved. He smiled. He fixed a fence for an old woman down the road. He gave rides to teenagers who needed to get to town. Nobody suspected. Not once. That is the horror of Donald Gins. Not the graves, though the graves are horrifying. It is the completeness of the disguise. It is that a man could kill dozens of people, most of them in the same 50-mi radius over more than a decade, and still be to every waitress and mechanic and preacher who spoke to him the polite little man from Prospect. The mask began to slip in 1975. That November, Gaskins killed a young man named Silus Yates, a farmer he had been hired essentially as a rural contract killer to eliminate. Two accompllices watched him do it. One of them, Walter Neely, was a slowwitted man Gaskins had used for years as a kind of pet witness. When the investigation into Yates's disappearance began pressing Neely, he broke. He told police that Peewee Gaskins had killed Yates. And then almost as an afterthought, he mentioned that Gaskins had killed other people, many other people, and that he could show investigators where they were buried. On December 4th, 1975, deputies followed Neie to a piece of land in Prospect. There, in a shallow patch of ground Gins had used as a private cemetery, they began to dig. They found the body of a woman named Jesse Ruth Judy. They dug further. They found her husband. They found a young mother and her two-year-old daughter. Over the following days, they found more. Eight bodies in the end in that first burial ground alone. And behind every one of them was the small, smiling man who had rented a house nearby, who had taught Sunday school for a season, who had fixed the sheriff's brother's carburetor two summers earlier. When Gaskins was arrested, he did not shout. He did not run. He simply seemed, in the words of one deputy, tired, as if a private household chore had at last caught up to him. His trial began in 1976. He was convicted of eight murders and sentenced to death. That sentence was commuted to life when the US Supreme Court briefly struck down the death penalty as applied. But Gaskins did not stop. Even in prison, the second face refused to sleep. In 1982 on death row at the Central Correctional Institution in Colombia, he accepted payment from the family of a murder victim to kill Rudolph Tiner, the young man who had killed their parents during a robbery. Gaskins rigged a small radio with plastic explosive and passed it to Tiner through the bars, telling him they would speak on it cell to cell. When Tiner held the radio to his ear, Gaskins detonated it. It is the only confirmed case in modern American history of a death row inmate murdering another death row inmate. For that killing and for the confessions that followed, Gaskins was returned to death row under a fresh sentence. In the last years of his life, he gave a lengthy, notoriously graphic confession to a writer in which he claimed to have murdered as many as 110 people. Investigators believe the true number is far lower, closer to 14 confirmed, and perhaps another dozen strongly suspected. But even that lower figure makes him the most prolific serial murderer South Carolina has ever produced. On September 6th, 1991, Donald Henry Gaskins was executed in the electric chair. He was 58 years old. He had lived his entire adult life within a 100 miles of the small dirt lanes where he had first learned to be benettin and to beat back. On the morning of his execution, guards said he ate a last meal and joked politely about the weather. The little man walked to the chair on his own two feet, waved once at a witness who had come to see him die, and sat down. The more ordinary pee-wee Gaskins tried to appear, the more disturbing what he had actually done becomes. Number two, Dand Storm Roof. On the evening of June 17, 2015, the young man who walked into Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in downtown Charleston looked to the 12 people gathered for Wednesday Bible study like nothing more than a shy visitor. He was thin, pale, 21 years old, wearing a gray sweatshirt and a b- cut haircut so unfashionable that several of the women present said later they had felt a maternal impulse to feed him. Reverend Clementa Pinkney, the pastor and a South Carolina state senator personally welcomed him and offered him a seat next to him in the fellowship hall. Someone handed him a Bible. He was invited to join the study of the Gospel of Mark. He sat for nearly 45 minutes among people who took him at face value as a stranger seeking God. The visitor was Diland Storm Roof, and every moment of that quiet welcome, every prayer, and every gentle question directed at him would afterward be studied as evidence of just how thoroughly a young American mass murderer had learned to hide inside politeness. ROF was born on April 3rd, 1994 in Colombia, South Carolina. By the accounts of teachers and relatives who spoke after his arrest, he was not a violent child, not a bullied child, not a child who set fires or hurt animals. He was, if anything, forgettable. He drifted through Colombia schools without leaving strong impressions on anyone. He tried white null high and later a second school. He never graduated. Neighbors described him as painfully quiet, a boy who mumbled hells in driveways, a boy who sometimes wore Confederate imagery on his jacket, but who also sometimes did not. He seemed harmless, aimless, a little sad. He seemed like exactly the sort of drifting young man that adults around him worried about only in the mildest way. That external mildness masked a private life of profound and organized racial hatred one roof had been constructing largely alone in front of a keyboard for at least 2 years before the massacre. According to the manifesto later recovered from a website he had registered. His radicalization began after he searched online for information about the killing of Trayvon Martin. From there, by his own account, he fell into white supremacist material of the crudest kind. He was not recruited. He did not attend rallies. He did not, so far as investigators could establish, belong to any organized movement at all. He was radicalized entirely by himself in his bedroom over hundreds of hours of screen time no adult in his life ever supervised. And this is the terrible duality of Dilan Roof. In the daytime, he was the boy in the sweatshirt, quiet in restaurants, forgettable at the counter of a gas station. At night, he was constructing a document filled with slurs, statistical distortions, and delusional history in which he had convinced himself that a race war was imminent and that someone somewhere had to start it. He photographed himself in the woods holding a Confederate battle flag. He photographed himself with a Glock 41 handgun his father had given him as a 21st birthday gift. He photographed himself standing on an American flag. Then he went back inside and helped his mother move a couch or watch television with a childhood friend, and no one who saw him in those daylight hours had any idea. In the month before the attack, he told at least one friend that he was planning to shoot black churchgoers. The friend did not believe him. He said Dylan talked strangely sometimes and drank too much and would sober up. ROF had also been arrested twice earlier that year, once for trespassing at a mall and once for possession of a controlled substance. Both encounters produced records, but no warning bells loud enough to reach the federal background check system that would later catastrophically allow him to buy the pistol he used at Emanuel Ame. He chose Charleston deliberately. He would later tell the FBI he chose it because of its history, because of its size, because of its symbolism as one of the cradles of American slavery. He chose Emanuelme specifically because it was one of the oldest black churches in the American South, founded in part by Denmark Vizy, whose planned 1822 uprising had ended in his execution not a mile from the church's front door. ROF had studied the church. He had visited Charleston before, driving down alone, walking the historic district, sitting in coffee shops with a laptop. To the tourists around him, he was a young man on a road trip. To himself, he was reconoitering an execution site. On the afternoon of June 17, he drove into Charleston again. He parked on Calhoun Street. He carried in a fanny pack the Glock 41 and eight magazines of hollowpoint ammunition. He walked to the church's fellowship hall entrance and asked for the pastor. He was welcomed inside as a stranger. He sat. He listened. He accepted a paper cup of water. He watched Reverend Pinkney open the Bible. And then at about 9:00, as the group bowed their heads for closing prayer, Dylan Roof stood up and began shooting. He murdered nine people in the space of a few minutes. Reverend Clementa Pinkney, Cynthia Marie Graham Herd, Susie Jackson, Ethel Lee Lance, Depay Middleton, doctor Taiwan Sanders, Daniel L. Simmons, Shironda Coleman Sinkulk, and Myra Thompson. He shot several of them multiple times. He shot the youngest as he tried to shield an ant. He shot the oldest as she prayed. Five people in the room survived. One of them, Polly Shepard, was told by ROF that he was letting her live so she could tell the world what had happened. Another survivor was a small child whose mother covered her body with her own and whispered to her to play dead. ROF left the church, got back into his black Hyundai Elantre, and drove north into North Carolina. He was captured the next morning near Shelby, North Carolina after a florist named Debbie Dills spotted his car on US 74 and followed him at a distance. On the phone with police until officers could make the arrest, he surrendered without resistance. In the back of the police car, he asked for food. Officers stopped at a Burger King on the way to booking and bought him a burger, an act that would later become one of the strangest and most discussed footnotes of the case, because it forced the country to see again and again the plain, mumbling, hungry face of the same young man who a few hours earlier had methodically executed nine people at prayer. His federal trial began in December 2016. Roof represented himself during sentencing, an unusual and legally destructive choice that his own attorneys, one of whom was the famed capital defender David Brookke, urged him not to make. He called no witnesses. He offered no mitigation. He said in a brief written statement that there was nothing wrong with him psychologically. He was convicted on 33 federal counts, including hate crimes resulting in death, and sentenced to death. In a subsequent state proceeding, he pleaded guilty and received nine consecutive life sentences. What made the case such a lasting shock in South Carolina was not only the crime itself, but the astonishing response of the survivors and the victim's families. Two days after the shooting, at ROF's bond hearing, several family members addressed him directly by closed circuit video. They spoke of forgiveness. They spoke of prayer. They spoke, in one case, of an 8-year-old granddaughter who had watched her grandmother die and who deserved a world in which people did not hate one another. The moment was broadcast across the country. It reframed the aftermath of the massacre in a way almost no other American mass killing has been reframed. Within weeks, the Confederate battle flag, which had flown over the grounds of the South Carolina State House for more than half a century, was lowered for the last time and removed permanently in direct response to the photographs. Roof had staged of himself with that same flag. The mask Dylan Roof had worn, the invisibility of the mild young man in the sweatshirt, had been chosen by him, not despite his ideology, but because of it. He had understood, with a cold and specific clarity, that he could kill more people in a black church if he did not look like a threat. He had used the assumption of harmlessness as a weapon. That understanding, once articulated in the record of his own writings and interrogations, made his crime particularly hard to metabolize. It was not the act of a monster who looked like a monster. It was the act of a young man who had learned to make himself look like a boy. He remains on federal death row. The more forgettable Dialan Roof tried to appear, the more monstrous the rest of the story becomes. Number three, Steven Stano. When most people in South Carolina first heard the name Steven Stano, they did not associate it with violence. To neighbors and casual acquaintances, he appeared to be an ordinary man living an ordinary life. He held jobs, maintained relationships, and blended into the communities where he lived. Nothing about his outward appearance suggested that investigators would later connect him to a series of violent crimes that shocked the state. What made the case so disturbing was not only the crimes themselves, but how easily Stano appeared to fit into everyday life. Friends described him as quiet. Others remembered him as polite and approachable. Yet behind that ordinary image, investigators would eventually uncover a pattern of manipulation, violence, and deception. Steven Stano was born in 1968 and spent much of his life in South Carolina. Like many offenders who later become the focus of major criminal investigations, his early years did not immediately predict what would happen decades later. By adulthood, he had built relationships, worked different jobs, and moved through several communities without attracting widespread attention. During the early 2000s, however, investigators would begin piecing together evidence linking him to multiple violent crimes. Authorities eventually connected him to two murders committed in South Carolina. In addition to those killings, he was convicted of several other serious offenses involving violence against women. One of the most significant cases involved the murder of his longtime girlfriend, Laura Ling. Investigators determined that the killing occurred in Horry County. After her death, evidence showed that Stano attempted to hide the crime and avoid immediate detection. Detectives carefully reconstructed the timeline through witness interviews, forensic evidence, and physical clues left at the scene. As investigators continued examining his activities, they discovered another victim, Henry Turner. Turner was killed during a separate incident in Georgetown County. Authorities concluded that robbery was one of the motives connected to the crime. By this stage, detectives realized they were dealing with a suspect responsible for multiple acts of extreme violence across different locations. The investigation expanded rapidly. Law enforcement agencies from several jurisdictions worked together, comparing evidence, interviewing witnesses, and tracing Stano's movements. Every new piece of information helped establish a clearer picture of what had happened. One important aspect of the case was the role of forensic evidence. Investigators relied on crime scene analysis, witness statements, and physical evidence rather than assumptions. Those findings became central during the prosecution and helped establish the sequence of events presented in court. When Stano was arrested, prosecutors charged him with multiple offenses, including murder. Court proceedings examined extensive evidence gathered during the investigation. Jurors heard testimony from investigators, forensic experts, and other witnesses who explained how the crimes had been reconstructed. Ultimately, Steven Stano was convicted in connection with two murders and several additional violent crimes. He received death sentences for the murders along with other lengthy prison sentences related to his remaining convictions. The case remains one of the better known modern murder investigations in South Carolina because it demonstrated how an individual who appeared unremarkable in everyday life could be responsible for devastating acts of violence. It also highlighted the importance of coordinated investigative work, forensic science, and persistence by law enforcement. For the families of the victims, however, the case has never been about headlines or courtroom decisions. It has always been about the lives that were lost and the lasting impact those crimes left behind. Their loss continues to be remembered long after the trials ended. Steven Stano remains on death row in South Carolina. His case is still referenced in discussions of major criminal investigations within the state, not because of notoriety, but because it serves as a reminder of how difficult violent crimes can be to detect and how essential careful investigative work is in bringing offenders to justice. More than anything, this case illustrates that appearances alone reveal very little about a person's actions. Communities often remember the ordinary public image while investigators focus on evidence, facts, and accountability. That evidence ultimately determined the outcome of the case and ensured that those responsible faced the justice system. As South Carolina continues to reflect on its criminal history, the Stano case remains a sobering reminder that behind seemingly ordinary lives, serious crimes can sometimes remain hidden until determined investigators uncover the truth. Number four, Patrick Tracy Burus. In the summer of 2009, residents across northern South Carolina were shaken by a series of seemingly unrelated shootings. Small towns that rarely appeared in national headlines suddenly found themselves at the center of one of the state's largest manhunts. Elderly residents, business owners, and local families were left wondering whether the next attack could happen anywhere. At first, investigators did not know if the cases were connected. Each crime scene presented its own challenges, and there was little to suggest that a single individual was responsible. But as detectives gathered evidence, compared ballistic reports, and interviewed witnesses, a disturbing pattern slowly emerged. The investigation eventually focused on Patrick Tracy Burus, a convicted violent offender who had recently been released from prison. Authorities later concluded that Burus was responsible for a series of fatal shootings across South Carolina during a crime spree that lasted only a matter of days. According to investigators, five people lost their lives during the attacks. The first victim was Klein Cash, a 63-year-old peach farmer who was found fatally shot on his property near Gaffne. Friends and neighbors described him as hardworking and wellresected in the community. Detectives initially searched for evidence of robbery and examined anyone who might have recently visited the farm. Only a short time later, another tragedy struck. Hazel Linder, an 83-year-old woman, was killed at her home. Her daughter, Gina Linder Parker, was also shot during the same attack and later died from her injuries. Investigators now had multiple homicide scenes that appeared to share important similarities. The violence continued when Steven Tyler, the owner of a local furniture store, was shot during a robbery. His 15-year-old daughter, Abby Tyler, was critically injured and later died despite medical treatment. By this point, fear had spread across Cherokee County. Businesses closed early, residents avoided traveling alone, and law enforcement agencies increased patrols throughout the region. Officers from local departments worked alongside the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division and other agencies to determine whether all of the shootings had been committed by the same suspect. A major breakthrough came through forensic analysis. Ballistics experts determined that shell casings recovered from multiple crime scenes had been fired from the same firearm. This evidence allowed investigators to officially link the murders into a single investigation. As detectives reconstructed the suspect's movements, they identified Patrick Tracy Burus as the primary suspect. Burus had an extensive criminal history and had been released from prison only months before the shootings. Authorities immediately launched an intensive manhunt, distributing his photograph across South Carolina and neighboring states. while warning the public not to approach him. The search ended on July 5th, 2009 when law enforcement officers in North Carolina responded to a burglary report. During the encounter, Burus exchanged gunfire with officers and was fatally shot. His death brought the manhunt to an end, although investigators continued reviewing evidence to confirm the full extent of his involvement in the killings. In the years since, the 2009 Gaffne murders have remained one of the most significant modern criminal investigations in South Carolina. Beyond the headlines, the case is remembered for the lives that were lost, the communities that were affected, and the coordinated investigative work that ultimately connected the crimes through forensic evidence. Number five, Susan Smith. There is a photograph taken by the local newspaper in Union, South Carolina in the last week of October 1994 that shows a young woman standing in front of a microphone with her hand pressed to her mouth. She is 23 years old. Her hair is pulled back. She is crying. Behind her stands her husband, David, his hand on her shoulder, his face also collapsing. She is speaking to a national television audience, begging the man she says has taken her two little sons at gunpoint to please, please bring them home. Michael is three, Alex is 14 months. She looks to every viewer like the picture of a mother in torment. The mother in the photograph is Susan Lee Smith. 6 days after the photograph was taken, she would confess that there had never been a carjacker at all, that she had strapped both of her sons into the back seat of her burgundy 1990 Mazda Protege and had rolled the car into John D Long Lake with the boys still inside, and had stood on the boat ramp and watched her car sink into black water with her children in it, and had then calmly joged to the nearest house, and begun the largest and most sustained ained public lie in the history of South Carolina. Susan Smith did not look before those nine days in the fall of 1994 like a woman who could kill her own children. She looked to almost everyone in Union County like a bright church-going young mother who was doing her best in a difficult marriage. She had been salutatoran of her high school class. She had worked at the Wind Dixie. She sang in her church choir. She was married to David Smith, an assistant manager at the same Wind Dixie. And although the marriage was strained, and although the couple had recently separated, she was seen at the grocery store on Saturdays pushing a cart with both boys strapped into the child seat, and she was seen at potluck suppers, and she was seen at family cookouts, and she was seen and seen and seen as ordinary. But under the surface, Susan Smith carried a history that would become central to every attempt to explain what she did. Her father, Harry Vaugh, had killed himself when she was seven. Her mother remarried a wealthy union businessman named Beverly Russell. When Susan was 15, she told a school counselor that her stepfather had been molesting her. An investigation began. The family closed ranks. The investigation was dropped when her mother declined to press charges. The abuse, according to Susan's later court testimony, continued. She attempted suicide twice as a teenager. She grew into a young woman who craved male approval with an intensity that friends described later as almost desperate. She met David Smith at the Wind Dixie. She was 17. Within a year, she was pregnant with Michael. They married. Alex followed. The marriage was troubled from the start. Both partners had affairs. They separated in the fall of 1994. Around that same time, Susan began seeing Tom Finlay, the 27-year-old son of the owner of Conso Products, the largest employer in Union County. Find was wealthy, handsome, unattached, and from Susan's perspective, a life raft. She wanted him seriously. He did not want her seriously. On October 17th, 1994, Find wrote her a letter, formal and gentle, in which he told her he could not continue their relationship. Among his reasons, he included in a passage that would later be poured over by prosecutors and psychologists, that he was not ready to be a father to someone else's children. Susan read that letter. She read it several times, and within days, according to her later confession, she began to formulate a plan. On the night of October 25th, 1994, Susan drove around Union County for several hours with her sons in the back seat. She went to a Walmart. She went to a friend's house. She spoke to acquaintances. She was seen and seen and seen being a mother. Sometime after 9:00, she drove to the boat ramp at John D. Long Lake, a small unlit inlet used by fishermen and Baptist congregations for baptisms. She put the car in gear. She released the emergency brake. She stepped out. The Mazda rolled slowly down the ramp and into the water, its tail lights glowing under the surface for several long seconds before it sank. Michael and Alex, still strapped into their car seats, drowned. Susan then ran to the nearest house, a home occupied by a couple named Shirley and Rick Mloud, and pounded on the door, sobbing that a black man had carjacked her at the intersection of Highway 49 and had driven off with her babies inside. The next nine days are a case study in the way an ordinarylooking mass can hold for a while under enormous pressure. Susan Smith described her fictional carjacker in specific detail. She described his knit cap. She described the gun. She described how he had told her he wasn't going to hurt her. Union County Sheriff Howard Wells, a man who had known Susan since she was a child, ran the investigation personally. The county mobilized. Volunteers searched fields. The FBI joined. President Bill Clinton was briefed. Susan appeared on national morning shows with her husband, holding photographs of Michael and Alex, pleading, weeping, breaking down. She was in that period one of the most photographed women in the United States. The mask began to fail almost immediately, though the public did not know it. Sheriff Wells noticed inconsistencies in her account. Traffic light patterns at the intersection where she said the carjacking occurred did not match her story. The light she described as red could not have been red for the duration she claimed. Behavior specialists from the FBI, quietly reviewing footage of her interviews, believed she was performing. On November 3rd, 1994, Wells sat down with Susan in a small office at First Baptist Church in Union and told her that he did not believe her. He said it with kindness. She broke. She wrote a two-page confession by hand. It began, "When I left my home on Tuesday, October 25, I was very emotionally distraught. The revelation shattered the town of Union and pulled the country up short. There had been no carjacker. There had never been one. The nation had spent 9 days searching, praying, imagining for a criminal Susan Smith had invented. The photographs of her weeping now had to be reread. Every gesture, every trembling word, every collapse into her husband's shoulder became evidence not of grief, but of performance. Her trial began in July 1995. Prosecutor Tommy Pope sought the death penalty. The defense, led by David Brookke, argued that Susan was a deeply damaged young woman who had attempted to kill herself along with her sons and had lost her nerve at the last moment, releasing the break before she could get back in the car. Testimony from her stepfather, Beverly Russell, was heard, and Russell publicly acknowledged for the first time that he had sexually abused her. Psychiatrists described her as suffering from major depression and dependent personality disorder. On July 22nd, 1995, the jury convicted her of both murders. They then declined to sentence her to death. She was given life in prison with the possibility of parole after 30 years. In November 2024, three decades to the month after she drowned Michael and Alex, Susan Smith appeared before the South Carolina parole board for her first hearing. She was denied. Members of her son's family, including their father, David, spoke against her release. She remained in the Leath Correctional Institution, and the country remembered once again the young woman on the television screen who had asked strangers to help find children she herself had killed. The more sympathetic Susan Smith had appeared in front of those cameras, the more disturbing the truth behind her tears turned out to be. Number six, Nathaniel Roland. On the evening of March 29th, 2019, 21-year-old Samantha Josephson left a popular entertainment district in Colombia, South Carolina, expecting to meet the Uber she had requested after a night out with friends. It was a routine decision that millions of people make every day. She checked her phone, walked toward a black vehicle waiting nearby, and got inside. Investigators would later determine that the car she entered was asterisk not the ride share vehicle she had requested. The driver was asterisk Nathaniel David Roland Atoisk, a 24year-old Colombia resident with a history of prior criminal offenses. According to investigators and evidence later presented in court, Roland was driving a black Chevrolet Impala that resembled many rid share vehicles operating in the city that night. When Samantha's friends realized she had not returned home, concern quickly turned into a missing person investigation, her phone stopped responding and family members traveled to Colombia, hoping that she would be found safely. Law enforcement agencies immediately began gathering surveillance footage, reviewing digital records, interviewing witnesses, and tracing Samantha's last known movements. One of the most important breakthroughs came from rid share records. Investigators confirmed that Samantha's actual Uber driver had arrived at the pickup location, but never transported her. GPS data showed the legitimate driver had waited briefly before leaving after the passenger failed to appear. Detectives now knew that Samantha had entered a different vehicle. Surveillance cameras from nearby businesses captured a black Chevrolet Impala in the area at approximately the same time Samantha disappeared. Investigators compared the footage with witness statements and began searching for the vehicle. Less than 24 hours after Samantha was reported missing, search teams located her body in a remote wooded area in Clarendon County, roughly 65 mi from Colombia. The discovery transformed the investigation into a homicide case and prompted an even larger response from state and local law enforcement. As detectives continued collecting evidence, they identified Nathaniel Roland as the primary suspect. His black Chevrolet Impala matched the vehicle seen on surveillance footage. Investigators obtained search warrants and conducted detailed forensic examinations of both the vehicle and Roland's residence. According to testimony presented during the trial, forensic investigators recovered Samantha Josephson's blood inside the Chevrolet Impala. They also located her cell phone and other personal belongings connected to the investigation. DNA evidence, fingerprints, cell phone location data, and surveillance footage collectively formed a timeline that prosecutors argued clearly linked Roland to Samantha's disappearance and death. Detectives also recovered a child safety lock mechanism that investigators said prevented passengers from opening the rear doors from inside the vehicle. Prosecutors argued that once Samantha entered the car, escaping became significantly more difficult. Nathaniel Roland was arrested on March 30th, 2019, one day after Samantha disappeared. During the investigation, detectives reconstructed his movements using cell phone records, surveillance video, vehicle evidence, and witness interviews. Each piece of evidence helped establish the sequence of events presented to the jury during trial. In July 2021, after hearing weeks of testimony and reviewing extensive forensic evidence, a Richland County jury found Nathaniel Roland guilty of kidnapping and murdering Samantha Josephson. He was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. The case received national attention, not only because of the tragedy itself, but because it highlighted an important public safety lesson. Following Samantha's death, her family launched the asterisk, "What's my name?" campaign encouraging rid share passengers to verify the driver's identity, license plate, and trip information before entering any vehicle. The campaign has since been promoted by universities, law enforcement agencies, and ride share companies across the United States. Today, Samantha Josephson is remembered by family, friends, and classmates as an ambitious University of South Carolina student who plan to attend law school after graduation. Scholarship programs and public safety initiatives created in her memory continue to encourage safer ride share practices. For investigators, the case demonstrated how surveillance footage, digital records, GPS data, DNA evidence, and coordinated police work can rapidly identify a suspect and build a strong factual case in court. While the trial brought legal accountability, it could not erase the loss experienced by Samantha's family and the wider South Carolina community. More than anything, this case serves as a reminder that small moments of routine decision-making can carry unexpected risks. The legacy left by Samantha Josephson's family has transformed that tragedy into a nationwide effort to help prevent similar crimes and encourage safer travel for millions of people. Number seven, Timothy Ray Jones Jr. to the parents at the elementary school in Lexington County who dropped their children off in the morning line. Tim Jones was the tall, thin, slightly stressed father driving the silver Cadillac Escalade with three of his five children, buckled in the back seat, waving him goodbye. To his neighbors in the Red Bank community, he was the recently divorced dad, who had won custody of all five of his kids, an unusual outcome that most people took as evidence of how badly the marriage must have gone and how much the court had trusted him. To his employer, Intel, he was a bright and reliable computer engineer, the sort of employee who had passed high clearance background checks and who wrote software for one of the most valuable companies in the world. That was Tim Jones on the surface in August 2014. Underneath, according to the state's later evidence, he was disintegrating. Jones was born on December 28th, 1981, and grew up in Amory, Mississippi. He was described by relatives as a bright, if odd, boy whose home life had been troubled by his own parents' divorce and by episodes of behavior that in retrospect seemed to hint at emotional instability. He earned a degree in computer engineering. He married Amber Kaiser when they were both very young. Between 2005 and 2013, they had five children. Mea, the oldest, was 8 years old in August 2014. Elias was seven. Nton was six, Gabriel was two, Elaine Marie was one. The marriage broke down badly. Amber later described episodes of controlling behavior, of paranoia, of moments in which she felt afraid. In 2013, the couple divorced. In a decision that would later be scrutinized by courts and by the public, a South Carolina family court judge awarded Tim Jones primary custody of all five children. The judge cited concerns about Amber's own conduct during the separation. Amber was granted visitation. To the outside world, Tim Jones was now a single father raising five young children while holding down a demanding technical job. Neighbors saw him at the grocery store with a full cart. They saw him at the church nursery. They saw him at the elementary school. Some pied him. Some admired him. Almost no one saw what was happening inside the house on Reedi Fork Drive. His use of synthetic drugs, particularly synthetic marijuana known as spice, had escalated. His paranoia had deepened. He had, in the months before August 2014, begun to accuse the children of behaviors and moral failings that ranged from the improbable to the delusional. He was punishing them with escalating harshness. He was documenting what he considered their offenses in a notebook. Cowworkers noticed he seemed jittery. School staff noticed the children seemed tired. On August 28th, 2014, Tim Jones picked his children up from daycare and school as usual. Sometime that evening in the small ranchstyle home on Reedy Fork Drive, he killed all five of them. According to the state's evidence and his own subsequent statements, he strangled the four older children by hand or with a belt in sequence over the span of the evening. He drowned the youngest one-year-old Elaine in a bathtub. 6-year-old Natan, according to Jones's account, died first after being forced to do calisthenics as punishment until his small body gave out. When Jones realized Natan was dead, or when, as he would later argue, he could not accept that Natan was dead by his own hand, he decided in a burst of terrified logic that the other four could not be allowed to live to describe what had happened. He wrapped the children's bodies in trash bags. He loaded them into the escalade, and then, in the days that followed, he simply drove. He drove east through South Carolina. He drove south through Georgia. He drove west into Alabama. He drove into Mississippi. He drove into a strip of the country he half knew from his childhood. He slept in the car. He bought fast food. He stopped at gas stations. And in the back of the Cadillac Escalade, wrapped in plastic were five children. At times he lay down on the bags of trash containing them and slept. The bodies began in the late summer heat to deteriorate. The smell in the vehicle became overwhelming. On September 6th, 2014, 10 days after the killings, Jones was stopped at a police checkpoint in Smith County, Mississippi. Deputies noticed the smell immediately. They noticed blood and fluid. They noticed his behavior. They detained him. Under questioning, Timothy Jones Jr. told deputies where they could find the children. He directed them to a remote red clay hillside in Alabama where he had several days earlier thrown the five plastic bags over the edge of a dirt embankment. Officers recovered all five children. The case that followed took nearly 5 years to reach trial. Jones's defense argued that he was severely mentally ill, that he suffered from schizopeeffective disorder, that his drug use had triggered a psychotic break. Prosecutors argued that whatever his mental state, he had known what he was doing, had concealed his crimes, had transported the bodies across three states with awareness of what he was doing, and had killed his own children out of a mixture of rage, paranoia, and a punitive sense of possession over them. The children's mother, Amber Kaiser, testified. So did family members. So did co-workers who described Jones's careful, controlled, high functioning workplace persona in the very weeks in which he was at home sliding into the state that would end his family. The contrast was one of the most devastating pieces of testimony a South Carolina jury has ever heard. On June 4th, 2019, Timothy Jones Jr. was convicted of five counts of murder. On June 13th, 2019, the same jury sentenced him to death. The South Carolina Supreme Court upheld the sentence in 2023. What lingers in the Jones case beyond the specific horror of what happened in that small home on a summer night is how much of the tragedy was invisible to the outside world until it was too late. The neighbors, the co-workers, the church nursery volunteers, the teachers all had a version of Tim Jones. the man in the escalade in the dropoff line. The man who talked about coding, the man who apologized when he was late. None of them had the man who had been keeping a punishment notebook. None of them had the man driving across the deep south with the bodies of his children in the back seat. The more responsible Tim Jones was thought to be, the more incomprehensible the ruin behind that responsibility turned out to be. Number eight, Joseph Ernest Atkins. to the small community of Monarch Mills, a former textile village outside Union, South Carolina. Joseph Ernest Atkins was the returned veteran on Barnett Road. He had served in Vietnam. He had come home in the late 1960s with commendations and with wounds his neighbors could not entirely see. He was the son of Benjamin Atkins, a well-liked older man in the community. Joseph was on most days quiet, polite, a little slow to smile. If he sat on the porch drinking, so did half the men in the county. If he raised his voice inside the house on some nights, that too was not so different from other houses on Barnett Road. That at least was the version of Joseph Atkins that his neighbors chose to see. There were at the same time other things in his record that a more careful gaze might have seen. There was the death of his first wife, Angela, in 1970. He had been convicted of her murder. He had served a prison term for it. He had been parrolled. And he had come home to Barnett Road as if a man could serve 5 years for killing the mother of his children and then simply resume his place among the neighbors, as though nothing had ever happened. It is that resumption, that quiet reabsorption of a killer into a community that ought to have known better that makes Joseph Atkins one of the most quietly disturbing figures in South Carolina's late 20th century criminal record. Atkins was born in 1947. He grew up in the mill villages of Union County. He was drafted, served in Vietnam, and returned in the late 1960s. By many accounts, he came back changed. He drank heavily. He had episodes of paranoia and rage. He and Angela married young. There were children and in 1970, according to court records, he shot Angela to death inside their home. He was arrested. He was convicted. He was sentenced to prison. He served roughly 5 years and was parrolled in the mid 1970s. The parole itself was not unusual for the era. What was unusual in retrospect was how completely the community around him allowed him to slip back into the role of ordinary neighbor. He remarried. He lived down the road from his aging father, Benjamin. He worked odd jobs. His father, in particular, appears to have been determined to see the best in him. Benjamin bought him things. Benjamin lent him money. Benjamin looked away. The next 15 years are the period in which the mask held. Then, on the night of November 21st, 1985, everything Joseph Atkins had been hiding, or perhaps had been slowly building, erupted at once. He had been drinking heavily, and using PCP, he got into an argument with his father, Benjamin. He shot his father to death inside the older man's home on Barnett Road. Almost immediately afterward, in the same rage or in a widening spiral of one, he went across the road to the home of his neighbors, the Pattersons. 15-year-old Karen Patterson was babysitting her younger siblings. Atkins forced his way into the house. He shot Karen. He took her body. He held law enforcement at bay through the night by threatening to detonate a homemade explosive. When the standoff ended, Karen Patterson was dead. Atkins was arrested. He was tried. He was convicted of the murders of his father, Benjamin, and of Karen Patterson. He was sentenced to death. 14 years of appeals followed. And on January 23rd, 1999, Joseph Ernest Atkins was executed by lethal injection in South Carolina. What is most disturbing about the Atkins case is the length of the silence between the first killing and the last. from the perspective of most of his neighbors on Barnett Road and from the perspective of his own father, Joseph Atkins in the mid 1980s was a man with a bad history who had done his time and who deserved to be treated as if he were again a member of the community. That treatment lasted for over a decade. During that decade, Atkins, by all accounts, held down work sporadically, took care of himself in the most basic ways, and did not, so far as the record shows, kill anyone. The mask, in other words, held perfectly for as long as it needed to hold until the private currents underneath it, whatever mixture of untreated post-war trauma, addiction, and violent character had produced the first murder, surfaced again, and swept two more lives away with them. There is no evidence in the trial record or in the appellet opinions that anyone in the community had felt themselves to be at particular risk from him in the years leading up to November 1985. He was up to the moment he was not simply Joseph. He waved. He worked. He drank. He was there. The more forgotten his past was allowed to become, the more monstrous the return of it proved to be. Number nine, Quincy Jovin Allen. At 22 years old in the summer of 2002, Quincy Allen was, to the people who saw him around the Colombia neighborhoods where he lived, just another young man drifting between low-wage jobs and rented rooms. He worked at a fast food restaurant. He rode buses. He was polite when spoken to. He carried a small notebook. He was the sort of quiet, unremarkable presence at the edge of a laundromat or a convenience store that no one upon being questioned later could describe in more than three sentences. He would later tell a court without emotion that he had begun killing that summer because he wanted to and because he enjoyed it. Allan was born on November 7th, 1979 in Colombia, South Carolina. His childhood was, by every clinical account entered into his trial record, a catalog of abuse and neglect that would have destroyed most adults, let alone most children. He was subjected to severe physical and sexual violence in the home by multiple perpetrators. Over years, he was placed briefly in foster care. He was returned. The abuse resumed. He was diagnosed at various points during his youth with post-traumatic stress disorder with major depression and with a range of dissociative symptoms. He dropped out of school. He worked odd job. He wrote in his private notebooks elaborate fantasies of violence. That inner life did not for most of his early adulthood break the surface. He was employed. He paid rent sometimes. He was capable of small, courteous conversation with the people who took his money at the bus depot or handed him a paycheck. He appeared from the outside to be simply another young black man in South Carolina's capital city, doing what he could. In July 2002, at the age of 22, Allan began a killing spree that would last less than a month. His first victim was Jedodiah Har, a young man he shot while Har was sitting in a car in Colombia. Days later, he entered a used car lot in Colombia and shot Dale Hall, a salesman, killing him. He set the body on fire. He also shot a woman named Tavar's Latrell Boyd who survived. Then he traveled south into Georgia. There in the small town of Sury, he shot two additional victims, killing them and burning them as well. He was arrested shortly afterward. In in statements to law enforcement and in a later interview with a psychologist that would be quoted at his sentencing, Allen spoke about the killings in a way that stunned everyone in the room. He described enjoying them. He described feeling in his own words that he was getting even. He described a sense of power that had eluded him for most of his life and that he had at last found. He did not attempt to portray himself as insane. He did not attempt to portray himself as remorseful. A psychologist who evaluated him said in open court that he would kill again if he could, that he liked it, that the community had no reason to expect that anything about him would change. Allan pleaded guilty in South Carolina in 2005 to two counts of murder, assault, and battery with intent to kill, and arson. He was sentenced to death in South Carolina. Georgia authorities also secured convictions for the two murders committed there and sentenced him to life. His South Carolina death sentence was overturned in 2022 by a federal court on grounds of ineffective assistance of counsel during the original sentencing phase. In 2024, he agreed to a resentencing that gave him life without parole. He is now serving that sentence. The contrast at the heart of the Allen case is not the contrast of a respectable public face and a hidden private one. Allan was never respectable in any conventional sense. He was before the killings invisible, another poor young man passing across the field of vision of a busy southern city. The contrast is between how utterly ordinary that invisibility looked and how completely it concealed a young man who was by his own confession hunting. In the years since his sentencing, criminologists have used the Quincy Allen case in academic discussions of childhood trauma, of dissociation, and of what happens when a society fails a child so thoroughly that by the time the child becomes an adult, he has nothing recognizable left to lose. That analysis is not offered here as excuse. Allan himself refused at sentencing to offer it as excuse. It is offered as context for the specific horror of watching a young man tell a courtroom calmly and without artifice, that he had killed strangers because he wanted to know what it felt like, and that he had found that it felt exactly as good as he had suspected it would. The more unremarkable Quincy Allen had been allowed to seem, the more chilling the interior he described became. Number 10, James Robertson. Jimmy Robertson had grown up in one of the nicer houses in Rock Hill, South Carolina. His parents, Earl and Terry Robertson, were both 49 years old in the fall of 1997. Earl worked in banking. Terry was known around the York County community as a warm, sociable woman who kept up with her neighbors and doted on her only son. Jimmy was 26. He had been given, by the standards of nearly any American family, every advantage. He had grown up in a stable home. He had had a car in high school. He had had money in college. He had a father who kept trying with patience most sons never receive to give him one more chance. That patience is the mask underneath which the murders in the Robertson family concealed themselves for as long as they did. Because to almost everyone who knew Earl and Terry, Jimmy was simply the disappointing son. Not the dangerous son, not the son to fear. The kind of son that mothers in the neighborhood clucked their tongues about at the mailbox. Robertson was born on July July 25th, 1971 in Rock Hill. By his mid20s, he had developed a pattern of drift and dependence that appears in family testimony from his own trial. He had attempted college and abandoned it. He had held jobs briefly. He had lived off and on at his parents' home when other arrangements failed. He liked to spend money. He liked to think of himself as a person who deserved money. Behind the passive charm he presented to his mother's friends according to trial testimony was a young man who blamed his parents constantly and privately for what he considered the modesty of the future they were offering him. In the autumn of 1997, the plan he developed for that future became the most shocking family murder case in York County's modern history. On the evening of November 30th, 1997, Jimmy Robertson entered the family home in Rock Hill, knowing that both of his parents would be present. He killed his mother, Terry, first, bludgeoning her with a clawhammer. He killed his father, Earl. Next, striking him with the claw end of the same hammer and a wooden baseball bat. The forensic account entered at trial was extraordinarily brutal. Both parents suffered dozens of separate wounds. Neither would have died quickly. Robertson then attempted to make the scene look like a robbery. He took jewelry. He took his mother's car. He set the house on fire, hoping the fire would erase the physical evidence. But the fire did not fully take. Neighbors saw smoke. Firefighters arrived quickly. The bodies of Earl and Terry Robertson were recovered largely intact. And within a very short time, investigators had begun to piece together a story in which the only person who benefited financially from the deaths of Earl and Terry Robertson was their son. Robertson was arrested. He was tried in York County in 1999. The evidence against him was overwhelming. He had made statements to acquaintances both before and after the killings that indicated he had been considering the plan for weeks. He was convicted of both murders. On June 3rd, 1999, he was sentenced to death. He has in the more than two and a half decades since remained on South Carolina's death row. In recent years, according to reporting by the Herald in Rock Hill, he has at times sought to abandon his appeals. He has said through council that he does not wish to spend the rest of his life inside the confined conditions of the state's death row. He has watched friends inside the unit be executed. He has at various points requested to be executed himself. As of the most recent public court filings, his case remained active. What separates the Robertson case from the more sensational murders that dominate South Carolina true crime histories is the ordinariness of its motive and the specificity of its concealment. There was no ideology. There was no mental illness of the sort that reshapes a case. There was in the end an entitled adult son with a plan to inherit willing to spend an evening in the house he had grown up in swinging a hammer and a baseball bat at his own parents. And there was on the outside before the murders the quiet young man in Rock Hill whom other mothers described only and only with mild exasperation as spoiled. That is the true final horror of the case and in a sense the horror that unites every entry in this ranking. Whether the mask is a small polite mechanic in Prospect or a mumbling college dropout in Colombia or a distinguished low country lawyer or a stressed single father in Lexington, the pattern is the same. What made these 10 criminals particularly dangerous and what allowed most of them to kill more than once was the very ordinariness of their public presentation. Communities look past the ordinary. That looking past is where every one of these cases lived for as long as it was allowed to live. The more unremarkable a person insists on appearing, the more carefully worth remembering the story behind that appearance can turn out to
fullTextVi: Số một, Donald Henry Gaskins. Đối với những người hàng xóm đã nhìn thấy anh ta trên cánh đồng của Hạt Florence, anh ta là một người đàn ông nhỏ bé, lịch sự, chăm chỉ, đội chiếc mũ rách nát, một người đàn ông có đôi chân bị tật không chạm tới bàn đạp của những chiếc xe tải mà anh ấy lái và giọng nói của anh ấy không bao giờ vượt lên trên Carolina mềm mại. Vẽ tranh. Anh ta được gọi là pee-đu là có lý do. Anh ta chỉ cao gần 5'5. Anh bắt tay bà ngoại ở cửa hàng tổng hợp. Anh ta sửa ô tô chỉ để kiếm từng xu. Anh ấy là kiểu đàn ông được nhiều người đàn ông khác tin tưởng chở con gái họ về nhà bởi vì anh ta có vẻ quá nhỏ bé, quá im lặng, quá tầm thường để có thể trở thành bất cứ thứ gì ngoại trừ vô hại. Đó là sự thật đầu tiên và đáng lo ngại nhất về Donald Henry Gaskins. Đối với hầu hết những người từng gặp anh một cách tình cờ, anh không chỉ đơn thuần là một người bình thường. Anh ấy đã được thông báo. Và người ta không hề nhận thấy rằng anh ta đã phạm phải chuỗi vụ giết người tồi tệ nhất trong Lịch sử tội phạm được ghi lại của Nam Carolina. Gaskins sinh ngày 13 tháng 3 năm 1933 tại Pine Flats gần Prospect, a rải rác những con đường đất ở Quận Florence mà ngay cả hầu hết người dân Nam Carolina cũng không thể tìm trên bản đồ. Mẹ anh có hàng loạt mối quan hệ với những người đàn ông bạo lực. Anh ta là con thứ năm trong số những người con của cô, không có ai cùng cha và không có trong số họ muốn có một cậu bé nhỏ nhắn, gầy gò luôn cản đường họ. Anh ta được lũ vẹt cấp dưới gọi khi còn nhỏ, sau đó chỉ đơn giản là tè dầm vì những kẻ bắt nạt sân trường không thể chống lại một mục tiêu nhỏ như vậy. Anh ta bị đánh ở nhà. Anh ấy bị đánh ở trường. Anh ta bị những người đàn ông say rượu trở về từ nhà máy tông vào đường. Bằng chính lời kể của mình, thế giới đã sớm dạy anh rằng mọi người đều nhỏ bé hơn mọi người tồn tại để bị đánh bại, và lối thoát duy nhất khỏi số học đó là tìm ai đó nhỏ hơn nữa. Anh bỏ học vào năm lớp bốn. Đến năm 11 tuổi, anh ta đột nhập vào nhà cùng hai cậu bé lớn hơn. Đến năm 13 tuổi, anh ta bị giam giữ ở tuổi vị thành niên vì tấn công một cô gái bằng rìu trong một vụ trộm không thành công. Và đến lúc anh được gửi đến Trường Công nghiệp Nam Carolina để học Các chàng trai, những tù nhân khác đã biết được điều kỳ lạ về Pee-Wee Gaskins, điều điều đó sẽ định nghĩa anh ấy trong bốn thập kỷ tới. Anh ấy trông như chẳng có gì cả. Nhưng khi anh ta bị dồn vào chân tường, bị sỉ nhục hoặc đơn giản là buồn chán, có điều gì đó đằng sau đôi mắt anh ta sẽ trượt sang một bên, và cậu bé lịch sự sẽ biến mất, và một thứ khác sẽ nhìn ra ngoài. Trong nhiều năm sau khi được thả, điều gì đó khác vẫn được giấu kín. Gaskins kết hôn khi còn trẻ. Anh ấy làm những công việc lặt vặt. Ông là cha của những đứa con. Khi thích hợp, anh ấy tham dự một nhà thờ nhỏ ở nông thôn, ngồi lặng lẽ trong ngồi xuống và gật đầu với các bài giảng. Anh ta được mọi người xung quanh Prospect biết đến như một người có thể vá mái nhà rẻ hơn hơn bất kỳ ai khác, và ai có thể được trông cậy để giúp đỡ một du khách bị mắc kẹt một chuyến đi nếu du khách không ngại mùi dầu trong taxi của chiếc Chevy của anh ấy. Anh ta có vẻ chính xác là người mà Quận Florence mong muốn ở vùng nông thôn, một người đàn ông tội nghiệp, vô hại, hữu ích. Bên dưới, số học đã quay. Gaskins sau này kể với một người viết tiểu sử rằng bắt đầu từ năm 1969, ông bắt đầu trải qua những gì anh ấy gọi là sự khó chịu, một áp lực tích tụ trong mắt anh ấy cho đến khi nó chỉ có thể được giải thoát bằng cách giết chóc. Anh ấy không mô tả nó như một cơn thịnh nộ. Anh ấy mô tả nó như là việc bảo trì hộ gia đình, một việc cần phải được thực hiện cách những người đàn ông khác tham dự vào hàng rào bị phá vỡ. Chiếc mặt nạ anh ấy đeo ở nơi công cộng gần như có độ chính xác như phẫu thuật. Khi Gaskins đón người quá giang dọc Quốc lộ 17 hay hai làn đường hẹp cắt qua vùng Low Country, anh ấy hay nói chuyện, xin lỗi, tự khiêm tốn. Anh ta nói với phụ nữ rằng anh ta có vợ và con ở nhà. Anh ta nói với mọi người rằng anh ta đang trên đường đi làm. Anh mời thuốc lá. Anh ta đề nghị trả tiền xăng. Anh khen nhẫn, đồng hồ, bốt. Anh ấy đã hướng chúng vào tâm trí của mình về cái mà anh ấy gọi riêng là những cuộc tàn sát ven biển của mình. Đây là những nạn nhân được chọn gần như ngẫu nhiên từ dải băng của Đại lộ phía Nam không được chia đoạn giữa Charleston và tuyến North Carolina. Đối với Gaskins, theo cách nói lạnh lùng của anh ấy, họ chỉ là những người mà tôi không quen biết. Anh ta bắn họ, đâm họ hoặc dìm họ xuống đầm lầy và chờ đợi chúng vào vùng nước đen nơi thủy triều và lũ cua sẽ xóa sạch những gì anh ta đã làm.
